Affiliate vs Partner vs Referral Programs: What's the Difference?

Guidelowob research

By lowob · 20 March 2026 · 6-minute read · Revenue

Affiliate, partner and referral programmes all pay other people to bring a company customers, but each needs different incentives and different measures. Affiliate programmes pay professional publishers a commission per defined event, at scale; US affiliate investment was about $13.6 billion in 2024. Partner programmes are fewer, larger deals negotiated between companies. Referral schemes give existing customers small rewards for bringing people they know, and the best study of them, at a bank, found referred customers were worth at least 16% more. Which one a company needs depends on who could plausibly send it a customer.

Three arrangements pay other people to bring a company customers. They share vocabulary, they are often run from the same software, and confusing them costs companies real money in the wrong terms offered to the wrong partners.

Affiliate programmes

An affiliate programme pays independent publishers a commission for customers they send. The publishers are professionals: comparison sites, review sites, content creators, newsletters, deal and coupon sites, and sub-networks that aggregate smaller publishers. They choose products to promote on the commission, the conversion rate and the fit with their audience, and they do it at scale, across many programmes at once.

The channel is large and diversifying. The Performance Marketing Association's 2025 industry study put US affiliate investment at about $13.6 billion in 2024, up 49.8% from 2021, supporting an estimated $113 billion in e-commerce sales. Retail's share of spend fell from 76% to 63% as financial services, travel and telecoms grew. This is trade-body research, and the release does not state its method.

The company sets the terms: what event is paid for, how much, for how long after the click, and what is prohibited. The programme lives on an affiliate network, which recruits publishers, tracks clicks and conversions and handles payments for a fee, or on a direct platform the company runs itself.

Affiliate is a performance channel in the strict sense. The company pays only when the defined event occurs. It scales with the number and quality of publishers recruited. It is available to many categories the ad platforms restrict, because publishers decide what to carry, though the publishers' own platforms and the category's rules still apply. The main risk is paying for customers who had already decided, which Build an affiliate programme without paying for coupon leaks covers in detail. The research is clear that the merchant should keep control: Edelman and Brandi found in-house staff were better than outside specialists at spotting "borderline" affiliates whose practices worked against the merchant.

Partner programmes

A partner programme is a relationship between companies rather than with individual publishers. Integration partners, resellers, agencies, platforms and complementary products agree to distribute, recommend or embed the company's product in exchange for revenue share, referral fees, co-marketing or reciprocal distribution.

Partner deals are fewer, larger and slower, and each is negotiated individually. A single partnership with a platform that already has the customer relationship can outweigh an entire affiliate programme. Partner programmes are run by people, not software; the tracking and payment tools matter less than the relationship and the terms.

The design questions are different from affiliate ones: what role the partner plays in the sale, how each partner type is paid, what tiers reward, and who owns an account both sides touch. Our Partner channel design works through those questions, What is a partner programme? defines the parts, and Integrators, OEMs and channel partners covers the main partner types.

Referral schemes

A referral scheme pays existing customers, or sometimes employees, for bringing in people they know. The reward is usually small, such as account credit, a discount or a bonus, and the volume per referrer is low, because each person knows a limited number of relevant others.

The evidence that referred customers are worth having is strong. Schmitt, Skiera and Van den Bulte tracked about 10,000 customers at a German bank that paid referrers a €25 voucher. Referred customers had a higher margin at first, a lasting retention advantage and at least 16% higher value over six years. The authors estimated a return of about 60% on the reward.

Reward size and context matter. Ryu and Feick's experiments found rewards raised referral likelihood most where ties were weak, and that a reward lifted referral likelihood by more than 20 percentage points for a weaker brand. Close friends refer without being paid. Referral works when the product is something people talk about anyway and the reward is enough to prompt the conversation without being enough to corrupt it. It is a product feature more than a marketing channel, and it is usually run from inside the product.

Ask who could plausibly send you a customer. The answer tells you which programme to build.

Which one a company needs

Ask who could plausibly send you a customer.

If the answer is professional publishers who already reach your buyer, such as comparison sites, creators and newsletters, you need an affiliate programme, with terms designed to exclude the coupon leak.

If the answer is other companies whose customers are your customers, such as platforms, integrations and service providers, you need a partner programme, and probably a person to run it.

If the answer is your own customers, you need a referral scheme, built into the product.

Most companies past a certain size need all three, run differently. Do not try to run a partner programme on affiliate software, or an affiliate programme with referral-sized rewards. Business-to-business introductions sit between the partner and referral models, and Referral partners without leakage covers how to register, protect and pay them.

Disclosure applies to all three

Each arrangement pays someone to recommend you, so each carries disclosure duties. The FTC's guidance says an affiliate should disclose the relationship clearly and close to the recommendation, that "affiliate link" alone is not adequate, and that advertisers need "reasonable programs in place to train and monitor members of their network." It also says a business cannot condition an incentive, such as a discount, on a review being positive. Regulated products add their own rules. Match customer referral rewards to the product and the applicable rules before launch.

Why they should be built and owned

Affiliate and partner programmes are among the few distribution channels a company can own outright. The terms, the partner base, the reporting history and the relationships are assets that keep working when any single ad platform changes its mind. For a company in a restricted category, they are usually the first thing worth building properly, and the last thing worth outsourcing to a network's default settings.

lowob takeaways

  • Pay affiliates for a clearly defined and verifiable outcome. Validate it with your own tracking.
  • Treat strategic partners as ongoing company-to-company relationships. Staff them with a person, not a dashboard.
  • Match customer referral rewards to the product and the applicable rules. Small, disclosed and built into the product.
  • Do not mix the tools. Partner programmes on affiliate software and affiliate programmes with referral-sized rewards both fail.

Common questions

What is the difference between an affiliate programme and a referral programme?

An affiliate programme pays professional publishers, such as comparison sites and creators, a commission per defined event at scale. A referral programme gives existing customers a small reward for bringing people they know, and usually runs inside the product.

What is the difference between a partner programme and an affiliate programme?

A partner programme is a negotiated relationship between companies, such as integrations, resellers and platforms, run by people. An affiliate programme is a set of public terms many publishers join, run on a network or platform.

Are referred customers more valuable?

The best evidence says yes. A study of about 10,000 customers at a German bank found referred customers were at least 16% more valuable over six years, with lower churn.

Do affiliate and referral programmes need disclosures?

Yes. In the US, the FTC expects paid relationships to be disclosed clearly and close to the recommendation, and advertisers to train and monitor their network. Regulated products may have extra rules.

Sources and notes

  • Performance Marketing Association, Industry Study 2025, 18 June 2025. Trade association research with London Research; methodology not stated in the release.
  • Schmitt, Skiera and Van den Bulte, Referral Programs and Customer Value, Journal of Marketing, 2011. Academic study of one German bank, 2006 to 2008.
  • Baylor University Keller Center, Referral reward programs and referral likelihood, 2008. Secondary summary of Ryu and Feick's Journal of Marketing experiments.
  • Edelman and Brandi, Risk, Information, and Incentives in Online Affiliate Marketing, Journal of Marketing Research 52(1), 2015. Academic study of affiliate program management.
  • FTC, Endorsement Guides: What People Are Asking, last updated July 2025. US staff guidance, not a rule.
  • The comparison table and the selection question are lowob's framework.
